question: On each side of a unit square, an equilateral triangle of side length \(1\) is constructed. On each new side of each equilateral triangle, another equilateral triangle of side length \(1\) is constructed. The interiors of the square and the \(12\) triangles have no points in common. Let \(R\) be the region formed by the union of the square and all the triangles, and let \(S\) be the smallest convex polygon that contains \(R.\) What is the area of the region that is inside \(S\) but outside \(R?\)
solution:
The useful observation is that the missing area is concentrated near the square's four vertices. Along any one side of the square, the first equilateral triangle and its two added triangles form a trapezoid. At the first triangle's outer apex, three \(60^\circ\) angles make \(180^\circ\), so the two exposed unit edges there form one straight segment of length \(2\).

At a square vertex \(V\), the square contributes \(90^\circ\), and the four triangles meeting there contribute \(4\cdot60^\circ\). The remaining gap therefore has angle
\[
360^\circ-90^\circ-4\cdot60^\circ=30^\circ.
\]
Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be the two outer tips bounding this gap. Then \(VP=VQ=1\). Joining \(P\) to \(Q\) fills the triangular gap \(VPQ\). Its other two angles are each \(75^\circ\).

These four gaps lie in the four separate exterior corner quadrants. Filling them produces a polygon whose boundary alternates between the four straight length-\(2\) segments and the four new joins. Each of its eight interior angles is \(60^\circ+75^\circ=135^\circ\), so it is convex. Moreover, any convex polygon containing \(R\) must contain each triangle \(VPQ\), since all three of its vertices belong to \(R\). Thus the filled polygon is exactly \(S\).

In one gap triangle, drop a perpendicular from \(Q\) to \(VP\). The resulting right triangle has hypotenuse \(VQ=1\) and a \(30^\circ\) angle at \(V\), so its height is \(1/2\). Consequently, each gap has area
\[
\frac12\cdot1\cdot\frac12=\frac14.
\]
The required area is \(4\cdot\frac14=\boxed{1}\), choice \(\mathrm{C}\).
